What I wanted to say is that my opinion is that perhaps an adequate personnel solution was not found, and therefore the commander was not appointed. They didn't find an appropriate person. They didn't find an appropriate personnel solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's what you wanted to say, then the matter has been clarified, Mr. Petrovic. Finally talking about last answers, about yesterday, your last answer yesterday, I'll read to you - and this is only the informal response at this moment - I'll read to you how it was translated to us initially, and then I'll read to you how the corrected translation is. You remember the sentence about the link and it was translated to us yesterday as follows: "Well, by virtue of their position they must have been linked. Somebody who is chief of sector or department and someone who is a special advisor or who occupies a certain position" - that was how it was translated to us yesterday. Now, the amended interpretation reads as follows: "Well, by virtue of their position they must have been linked in some way. Somebody who is chief of department and someone who is a special advisor and prior to that a chief ..." that is how the corrected translation is. Is there any need for you to further clarify or to explain or are you satisfied with how this translated now? I do understand now of course it's translated back to you. If you would like to listen to what you said yesterday, we could play it for you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there's no need, Your Honour. But yesterday it says someone who was chief of sector. You can see that here. The sector is something else. It's a narrow body. This is better today, but I think these were my words, someone who is chief or the deputy chief, and so on and so forth, but it's not necessary to go into all the details. I do agree with this. Someone who had a certain position in the service should have been familiar with such things. The translation is fine. I just didn't want this statement to be controversial in relation to what I have testified here. One of the accused was the chief of the service and the other was the deputy chief. I didn't want there to be any problems. I didn't want it to appear as if I had said something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We wanted to have your words clear on the record. Mr. Petrovic, the matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have heard the witness unless there is any other translation issue involved here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the latest problem is page 50, line 14, the chief of the service and the other was the deputy, but now it was not correctly interpreted. It doesn't say the deputy of what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat, Mr. Milosevic. One of the accused was the chief of the service, and the other you said was chief --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the deputy chief of the 2nd Administration; that means an administration within the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. If there are no questions further for the witness, this concludes your testimony, Mr. Milosevic. You've showed the -- no. Can we deal with the other matter when the witness has left or would we need to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: From my perspective we can. It was that I planned to tender the unsourced assertions agreement and we had offered the witness -- it's up to Mr. Petrovic. From my perspective, I think based on our agreement, I'm comfortable to tender it based on our discussions. If Mr. Petrovic disagrees, then I just wanted to raise it before the witness was excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, do we need the witness for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not quite sure about what my colleague has said. Why? Well, for the following reasons: First, I would like to explain the process that we were involved in, my learned friend and the Simatovic Defence. I understood the instructions and the purpose of the process, which is to assist colleagues from the Prosecution to do their work when cross-examining Mr. Milosevic. To that end, we met last Friday and we tried to answer as many questions as possible, questions put by my learned colleague. But these are the answers that we tried to provide on the basis of our knowledge without having consulted Mr. Milosevic. So what the document contains, the one discussed by my colleague, concern our attempts to interpret the sources that Mr. Milosevic had. As to whether our interpretation is adequate or not, well that is an open question. We have done our best to be of assistance, but as to whether everything is in accordance with Mr. Milosevic's position, well that can't be said. And there's one other thing I would like to point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to be clear. What apparently the Prosecution intends to tender is a list of assertions and with it the position of the Prosecution as far as the sourcing is concerned and the position of the Defence as far as the source or basis of knowledge or expert opinion is concerned. And it may be clear that this is not verified with the witness itself; it's just the interpretation of the parties. Have I understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think the matter is clear -- Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If it's the appropriate time, I'd like to object to that procedure. In our submission, it's an attempt by the Prosecution to make submissions at a time which is not appropriate and at a time when, one, we the Stanisic Defence have not had an opportunity to contribute; and two, many of those comments relate to paragraphs which may, in fact, not be paragraphs where there's any contention between the Prosecution and Defence; and thirdly, it's an issue also for resources, that the Prosecution have a huge amount of resources. They can sit there drafting submissions and forcing the Defence into a position where they have to respond to them at this stage and it's an advantage which they ought not to be able to use. The time for submissions is coming up very soon and we can all make submissions about the reliability and the credibility of Mr. Milosevic's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it in any way bind the Stanisic Defence? You say this is not the time for argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we could have done the same with Theunens. We could sit there and make submissions and say to the Prosecution, You've got to respond now. I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether it's the position of the Prosecution that the Stanisic Defence was to respond now or that it's just put on the record what the position of the Simatovic Defence, who called the expert witness, and the Prosecution is; no more, no less, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, I'm not following what Your Honour just said. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, two parties apparently find it relevant to inform the Chamber as to their positions in relation to the sources, basis of assertions which these two parties have found in the report, leaving it entirely open whether the Stanisic Defence, at whatever time, would like to present a different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd understood -- maybe I've misheard, and I may well have done that. The Simatovic team objected to this as well. But if they don't then, well, I think I'll withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I missed it, as a matter of fact. It was -- let me check with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, all three of us understood the position of the Simatovic Defence as not opposing what their position is, although sometimes briefly explained in this chart. But if that is a misunderstanding, Mr. Petrovic, then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I wasn't sufficiently clear. I've tried to explain the procedure, the purpose, of what my learned friend and I did. The process and objective was to facilitate her cross-examination, and not to comment on the sources. I just wanted to be of assistance. I didn't want to state anything that might be considered to be evidence because I can't do that without the person who was the author. That's the first matter. So this document in itself is not reliable because it contains some of the Defence's positions that are perhaps adequate and perhaps aren't adequate with regard to what the witness would say if he was asked about this. And then secondly, my learned friend's approach is such that with regard to every sentence, with regard to every allegation, they want to have a source. They forget that this is an expert who expresses opinions, who bases this on his expert experience, and all of this cannot be referred to in a footnote. So this approach excludes the validity of this document. It seems that if there are hundreds of allegations that haven't been backed up and that's quite simply not the case because we have an expert witness here and the expert has his own knowledge and his own experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you want to say is that you object, after having explained what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In brief, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll -- then we don't need the witness any further for this. I think we should first excuse the witness. Ms. Marcus, you would agree that we can deal with the matter without the witness. Mr. Milosevic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way and for patiently answering all the questions that were put to you during quite a number of days. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next witness, Ms. Marcus, you said you intended to tender it. May I take it that you hereby have tendered it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's uploaded as 65 ter 6490. Now, the earlier version prior to our meeting was translated into B/C/S, but of course we made revisions to it jointly. So the revised version will have to be submitted for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] this -- that is this version, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think -- but the gist of the document the Chamber can assess on the basis of what we have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then would you like to add anything in support of admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Only to point out that frankly I understand Mr. -- I agree with Mr. Petrovic's assessment of what this is. These -- he did endeavour to assist us and we're -- appreciate that. These were assertions in the report which we couldn't determine what the source was. We just couldn't determine it. Now, it may be because we missed something, but that was the purpose of having our meeting. And as a result, a number of lines were taken out and the Defence had an opportunity to explain their position as to the parts of the report, which although we say are not sourced and there should have been a source, where their view is that his academic knowledge is the source, so his expertise. So I think this is -- this is a submission. I'm in the Chamber's hands as to whether it should be filed as a written submission or admitted as an exhibit for the Chamber's reference. And I think it's quite clear what this is. Now, with respect to Mr. Jordash's point about him not having had an opportunity, I'm in the Chamber's hands. It's true, he didn't join in the discussion. He may have the Stanisic Defence's view to input onto this. And so for that I leave that in the hands of the Chamber. I think it's quite clear -- I should also add one more point. This does contain a lot of information about what the potential sources are. Without this, the Chamber might not have access to those sources. It's a cross-referencing tool. Some of it is clearly explained and I left those in. We agreed to leave those in to assist the Chamber because some of Mr. Petrovic's guidance as to which paragraphs were actually sourced to the same document, et cetera, were quite helpful, in fact. So this is essentially a tool to assist the Chamber with the Prosecution and Simatovic Defence positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, your position was specifically referred to. Any further comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Only that it -- it's -- in our submission, it's just not fair that the Prosecution can effectively raise a subject during cross-examination -- during examination of a witness as if it's pivotal to the examination of the witness, and then having obtained the information from the Defence then say, Well, actually now it's a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, brief, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a few sentences. If someone claims that there are dozens or hundreds of allegations that haven't been backed up in the expert report, the best method to deal with the matter is to ask the person what the allegation is. The Defence was asked about this after the witness had taken the solemn declaration. The Defence has been doing its best, but the Defence has certain limits because we're in a different position from the position of the witness. And from what point of view the value of this material is limited, if non-existent. What the Defence thinks is -- perhaps is in accordance with what the witness might say, perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies admission of the document, Ms. Marcus. Now, of course it -- Madam Registrar, purely for the record, do we need to know what document was denied admission because then it has to -- if we have the 65 ter number, then we don't need --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can state, yes, that's the document 6490.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And admission is denied. Then I'm looking at the clock. I think we should take a break now, resume at 12.30, and then hear the next witness. But I can imagine that we'd first like to deal with the matter in private session for a second. But if there's anything else at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just wanting to note, it would be our request to deal with the documents in connection with this witness as soon as possible. I don't know what your -- what the Chamber was planning in terms of timing of that. There are quite a lot of pending exhibits that haven't been tendered, and Your Honour has requested that we be proactive in trying to not put things off for housekeeping sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So in line with Your Honour's instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We -- Madam Registrar, I think you have looked at the many documents on the list to be tendered. There was one double in it. There was one marked not admitted, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar needs a bit more time to digest the list which she received only this morning. That's -- and that time will be given to her. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one more sentence that maybe should have been uttered earlier. At the Prosecutor's request, the expert has prepared a list of literature and explanations. We received that through the Victims and Witnesses Unit. This has been uploaded as 2D1689 and I believe that this should be joined to the list of documents for admission. We still don't have a translation for the document. This is pending, but I believe that this will be provided shortly because the document was submitted through the Victims and Witnesses Unit on Monday, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pending translation, we'll of course not admit the document, but would there be any principled objection against having it admitted once the translation is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. In fact, we would also like it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then 2D1689 is marked for identification under what number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under number D853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we are waiting for the translation. Madam Registrar, the documents which were tendered by the Simatovic Defence, do we now have the -- have the parties received the list with the numbers and the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour. The list will be filed this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will be filed this afternoon. Then we'll decide once it's there on admission. Then finally I'd like to go and -- unless if you'd prefer to have the break now, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll start after the break briefly in private session. We take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to start with delivering an oral decision, which is the decision on the Prosecution's request to re-call Radenko Novakovic. Radenko Novakovic testified as a Stanisic Defence witness before this Chamber from the 4th to the 7th of October, 2011. During his testimony, the Prosecution indicated the possibility of a future request to re-call the witness in order to confront him with materials yet to be received from the Republic of Serbia. The Chamber subsequently instructed the witness not to communicate or speak about his past or future testimony until further notice of his possible re-call. The discussion and instruction can be found on transcript pages 14168 up to 14170 and 14221 of the trial transcript. On the 24th of April, 2012, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion seeking leave to re-call Witness Radenko Novakovic for further cross-examination. On the 1st of May the Simatovic Defence orally submitted that it did not oppose the motion. On the 3rd of May, the Stanisic Defence informed the parties and the Chamber through an informal communication, which is hereby put on the record, that it did not object to the re-call of Witness Novakovic. In its motion, the Prosecution seeks further cross-examination on witness-related documents that the Serbian authorities made available or made available in unredacted form only after the testimony of Witness Novakovic. The Prosecution also argues that the Stanisic Defence had not given proper notice of the elicited testimony and of related documents before the witness began to testify. Finally, the Prosecution wishes to question Witness Novakovic about a document relating to members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, which was purportedly authored by the witness but tendered by the Stanisic Defence only after his testimony, as well as to confront him with entries from the Mladic notebooks. Pursuant to the Tribunal's case law, a Chamber shall, in determining whether there are sufficient grounds to re-call a witness, consider whether the requesting party has demonstrated good cause to re-call the witness. In assessing good cause, the Chamber will consider the purpose of re-calling the witness and the applicant's justification for not eliciting the relevant evidence from the witness when he or she originally testified. In determining whether the Prosecution has shown good cause to re-call Witness Novakovic, the Chamber takes into account that the witness's personnel file was only received by the Prosecution on the 8th of November, 2011. Similarly, there were other documents that were provided to the Prosecution by the Defence only after the testimony of Witness Novakovic. The Chamber also considers that the Prosecution may not have been in a position to assess the relevance of previously redacted documents. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution was not fully able to question the witness in respect of the redacted document and was not able to question the witness at all in respect of the documents not yet in its possession. As regards the Mladic diary entries, the Prosecution has not explicitly argued good cause for why it did not put those to the witness at the time of his original testimony. Nonetheless, taking into account that there are no objections to the witness's re-call and the fact that the missing documents may also have hindered the Prosecution's ability to assess the relevance of documents already in its possession, the Chamber will not limit the parameters of the re-call in relation to the Mladic diary entries mentioned in the Prosecution motion. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber finds that the Prosecution has shown good cause to re-call Witness Radenko Novakovic and therefore grants the motion. The Chamber reminds the parties that they continue to be under an obligation to refrain from any contact with the witness prior to the conclusion of his testimony, as they have been since the 7th of October, 2011, when the Chamber gave its instructions to the witness. In addition, the Stanisic Defence is hereby instructed to ensure through the Victims and Witnesses Section that the witness is informed about this decision and that he appears directly after the conclusion of the testimony of the last Simatovic Defence witness. The Chamber also invites the Prosecution to inform as soon as possible the parties and the Chamber of the estimated time needed for the cross-examination of Witness Novakovic. This concludes the Chamber's decision. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Plahuta, you have already given your solemn declaration when we were in private session. You'll now first be examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Plahuta.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Before I commence, I would like to ask you that since we speak the same language, you should make a brief break between questions and answers so that the interpreters can correctly interpret my questions and your answers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. The interpreters are suggesting that I use this. With your leave, just a moment. Mr. Plahuta, be so kind to tell us for the sake of the transcript your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 10th of December, 1970, in Kladovo, in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your name is Dejan Plahuta. Do you have a nickname that you are known by?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Svabo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about your educational background. When did you complete your schooling?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed primary school in Bajina Basta where I enrolled in the secondary mechanical school. I didn't complete my education in that school. At the time I was more attracted by the army and by work. After the army I could complete my education later, which is what I subsequently did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, you completed or you interrupted your education in the secondary mechanical school, and what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I interrupted my education, I went to perform my military service in Knjazevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you performed your military service and when did you return from your military service and where to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I performed my military service in the very same year, in 1998 [as interpreted], September 1998, and I went to Knjazevac to perform my military service there. I spent several months there, and I was then sent to be a part of the border service, and that was at the border with Bulgaria. I returned one year later in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that you returned, where did you return in 1989?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1989 I returned to my place of residence which is Perucac in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, the transcript says that you went to perform your military service in 1988. Let's just try and correct that. Is that correct, when did you go to perform your military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Plahuta, when you returned to Bajina Basta, what did you do up until 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned to Bajina Basta, I found a job in a state-owned company called Pik Takovo in Gornji Milanovac. It had a branch in our area and that's where I found a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long you worked in that firm Pik Takovo and what happened when you left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in Pik Takovo for one year until the end of 1990. I was there for a year and then it was no longer necessary to work there because half of the company had stopped working and I then went to Bajina Basta for a military exercise. I was called to go to Bajina Basta for a military exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, this is just an introduction, but very briefly within which military unit were you? How long were you involved in this military exercise? And where was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent about two months in that military exercise. It was in Zaovine, and it was with the border service of the Uzice Corps because the Uzice Corps -- well, it covered our area, the whole area, Bajina Basta. Throughout the area we had the Uzice Corps. I remained there for about two months. This procedure was a regular procedure and every soldier would go through that procedure after he had performed his military service. This had to be done after a certain period of time had expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Afterwards were you called up again at some point in time to join the army, the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, afterwards, after that I was called up in 1992 and, no, earlier than that. Before that I worked in a company for a year. Then I was called to join the regular, active army, the Army of Yugoslavia or the JNA as it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this was, who called you up, and to join which unit? How did you join the unit in question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was perhaps in September 1992. They called us. There was some sort of a competition for contractor soldiers, for professional soldiers. I -- whoever responded would go to the military department in Bajina Basta, they would register there, and afterwards the individual would be deployed in units on the border at the Drina, and this was within the framework of the Uzice Corps naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you sign some sort of a contract with the Uzice Corps at the time; and, if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I signed a contract in October for a period of six months. I signed this contract with the Army of Yugoslavia. And at the time I was deployed in Bajina Basta in the village of Bacevci, and I was part of the border service or I think it was the Border Battalion of the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, for the sake of the transcript you said in October you signed a six-month contract with the army. In October of which year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you signed the contract you said that you were first in the village of Bacevci. What sort of duties did you have to perform there and where were you transferred to in order to complete the remainder of your contract there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent about a month, a month and a half, in the village of Bacevci and we went on patrol along the border by the Drina River there. Afterwards, as my place of residence was in Perucac, they helped me by sending me to Kralu [phoen] in Perucac about a month later. That was at the beginning of December of the same year. Naturally, I had the same duties. I had to go and patrol and protect the state border there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, when your contract with the army expired, did you extend it; and, if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not extend it. I did not extend my contract with the army. I had a minor clash with an officer in relation to a certain incident, so naturally as my existence depended on this we went to see some officer who was responsible for that domain. We asked: Will we remain here after the contract has expired? Will we still have duties to perform? And then he was brazen and there was a squabble. He said, Why should I care about you? Something like that. My contract expired a few days earlier -- in fact, we left the Army of Yugoslavia before the contract expired, a few days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, while your contract was still valid and when you were in Kralu in Perucac, do you know whether there was an attack of any kind launched against Skelani and Bajina Basta; and, if that was the case, do you remember when it was launched?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it's the village of Skelani, it's the the border of our sector that our Kralu protected. Naser Oric attacked Skelani in January 1993. This was in mid-January at the time of the Serbian new year. I can't remember the exact date. Was it a day earlier or a day later -- but it was the 13th, 14th, 15th, or 16th. It was during that period that the attack was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any consequences of the attack for the bridge in Bajina Basta and for the town of Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fire was opened from a Browning 12.7-millimetre machine-gun. I think that was the calibre because the cartridges were found. The bridge and town were fired on and two mortar shells fell in the very centre of the town on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say in the very centre of the town, what town do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bajina Basta. Only a bridge separates Bajina Basta from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the population reacted to that attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population started fleeing the town over the next few days because fire was opened on several occasions and there was a random bullet trace here and there. People started looking for shelter. They started locking themselves in their apartments and the town was literally deserted. Only the troops were there, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was that an alert sounded and were there any other forces besides the regular army troops?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were on first degree -- or a first-level alert in our border-crossing service. We had to be prepared for combat. Everybody had to return from furlough, from vacation. They all had to return. And the police, together with us, stepped up their activities on the border crossing. They patrolled the area in their cars. They surveilled the area in certain places.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At the moment of attack where were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment of attack I was in Perucac in the barracks on the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The attack that we are discussing at the moment, did it result in the forces from Bajina Basta in the territory of Serbia crossing over to the territory of Skelani and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Over the next several days some elements of the Uzice Corps crossed over as well as the corps of the special forces of the Army of Yugoslavia. They were on the strength of the 63rd Parachute, the 72nd Brigade and the special brigade. Those were special forces in our army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said the 63rd Parachute, the 72nd Brigade, and you also mentioned a third unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did some police forces cross over?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No police forces crossed over. There was no need for them to cross over to the territory of a different state, to come to Skelani, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me how do you know that? How do you know that the police forces didn't cross over?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at my watch-tower, at my border crossing, we followed the rule according to which the soldiers and the officers at the watch-tower and the border crossing had to be kept up to speed. The commander thus told us which forces had crossed over and that the police were only doing their job on the other side, that we should co-operate with them, that we should agree with them as to what to do during night patrols, day patrols, if they put up their surveillance service we should not overlap with them. We were in contact all the time with the police, so I know -- I'm a hundred per cent sure that what I'm saying is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Uzice Corps, once the troops crossed the Drina River ended up in the territory of Skelani municipality, had some sort of co-ordination, some sort of relationship with some of the forces from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and based on what my commander told us, they relied on the Drina Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, can we now look at a document, 2D1667. While we are waiting for the document to appear on the screen, this seems to be a document issued by the Drina Corps on the 25th of January, 1993. It was sent to the command of the Uzice Corps to Drina OG through the 1st Army operations centre. It says here the Drina Corps is engaged in accomplishing the task's code name Proboj, and there is a reference to the contact line with the enemy. Do you know, are you familiar with the places mentioned in here, the villages of Kamenica, Cerska, Skugric, Pobudje, Slatina, Suceska, Gunjace, and Podrinje village. Do the names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of those villages. I know more or less where they are, but I've never been there so I can't tell you that. I know them, they do ring a bell. They're not far from the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what about the village of Sase, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I heard of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: A bit later I'm going to show you a map and we're going to try to locate those villages in that map. And now let me ask you, does it say in the penultimate paragraph: "We shall endeavour to cut the Zeleni Jadar-Zepa road." Do you know where Zeleni Jadar is? What road is this document about between Zeleni Jadar and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where Zeleni Jadar is. I know where Zepa is as well. Zepa is up the stream from our sector where we secured the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Plahuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to show the witness two or three more documents where some places are mentioned. And then I would like to ask the help of the witness to reconstruct the locations of those places in a map. Can we now look at 2D1670.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Mr. Plahuta, the document was compiled a day later on the 26th of January. It seems that the command of the Uzice Corps sent a dispatch to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to the command of the Drina Corps, that is. Tell us, please, before you look at the document, who was the commander of the Uzice Corps while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the second bullet point in this document, where it says: "Part of the forces used so far to provide artillery support will be retained on the right bank of the Drina River, from where we will lend support to your forces as per plan and request." First of all, do you know anything about the artillery support that was provided by the Uzice Corps to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was done at two places. One of those places was Oslusa on Tara mountain and the other one was the Perucac-Mitrovac road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, under 3 it says: "The Uzice Corps will continue operations in order to seize the most favourable features and positions. We will duly inform you of the time to take over the lines reached by way of a separate order." When we're talking about seizing the most favourable features and positions and lines reached, what part of the territory is meant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it was the part of the territory in East Bosnia, which they wanted to liberate from Naser Oric's forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now look at 2D1671.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, this is a telegram seemingly again from the commander of the Uzice Corps, Dragoljub Ojdanic. It was compiled on the 27th of January, 1993. Under 3 there is a reference to the line that the Uzice Corps had taken up. And it says: "Up until now we have inflicted losses on the enemy in the village of Mlecova, Jagodnja, Joseva, Daljegosta, Arapovici, Pavkovic, Tihici, Milicevici, Osmace, Tokoljak and Jezero." Are you familiar with these names? Do you know where these villages are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These villages are all in East Bosnia and they are all close. Some are closer and some are further away from the state border, but they are all in the same sector, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In here we can see that TG 2 will attack in order to take the village of Kusici, Kadrici, and further on towards the village that that attack will continue. Are you familiar with the names of the villages of Kusici as well as Jezero or the lake?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kusici does ring a bell. I'm also familiar with Jezero lake. Once upon a time a fair -- a village fair used to be held there. It's a plateau in East Bosnia and I'm familiar with the village of Kusici because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Plahuta, I just wanted to show you that map. My time is running out. I want to connect the three documents. I would like to call up for 2D1688. It's the map that I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But looking at the clock, Mr. Bakrac, I think the map has to be dealt with tomorrow because we'll adjourn for the day. Mr. Plahuta, we would like to see you back because we're not sitting tomorrow. We'd like to see you back in the afternoon of Monday, the 14th, at quarter past 2.00. I think it will be in the same courtroom, but you'll be informed about that. Madam Registrar says that we're in the same courtroom. I have to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or testimony still to be given next week, not only not to speak or not to communicate in any way with anyone about your testimony. Mr. Bakrac, I observed that the evidence you have elicited from the witness over the last ten minutes is whether the witness knows where certain places are and where these places are. I think one minute with the map could have provided that information. I do not think that there's much dispute between the Prosecution and the Defence about geographical matters. So therefore, whether we really have to show a map to the witness and spend another five or seven minutes to find out where these locations are, I wonder whether that's the most efficient way of proceeding. You asked him one question about the most favourable features. That was the one question of any substance and then the witness answered: I suppose. Apparently he was not familiar with the document. Could you please keep that in mind when preparing for the continuation of your examination-in-chief. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume Monday, the 14th of May, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in this same courtroom, 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of May, 2012, at 2.15 p.m.
